# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death. Landmark trials established its survival benefit: the second Multicenter Automatic Defibrillator Implantation Trial demonstrated that after an average follow-up of 20 months, prophylactic defibrillator implantation produced a significant 31% reduction in risk of death among patients with prior myocardial infarction and reduced ejection fraction [1], and the Sudden Cardiac Death in Heart Failure Trial extended this benefit to patients with congestive heart failure [2]. However, conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs) carry risks intrinsic to their endocardial leads. The risks of complications, in particular those related to lead failure and systemic infections, associated with traditional transvenous devices are an on-going concern [3].

## Rationale and Early Development

The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (S-ICD) was designed to avoid complications related to the transvenous ICD lead by using an entirely extrathoracic placement [4]. The first-in-human experience was reported in 2010, when Bardy and colleagues described an entirely subcutaneous cardioverter–defibrillator tested in a total of 78 patients, confirming feasibility of consistent defibrillation without intracardiac hardware [5]. Subsequent prospective evaluation in the IDE study established that the most frequent complications associated with ICDs involve the transvenous leads; a subcutaneous ICD was developed as an alternative system, and this study evaluated its safety and effectiveness for treatment of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [6]. A pooled analysis of the IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry showed that the S-ICD demonstrated high efficacy for VT/VF, with complications and inappropriate shock rates reduced consistently over follow-up [7]. Long-term EFFORTLESS data subsequently reported 5-year outcomes of registry patients with early-generation S-ICD devices, with analyses performed for mortality and late complications, appropriate shock and inappropriate shock rates [8].

## Inappropriate Shocks and Sensing Refinements

Early devices were limited by inappropriate shocks (IAS), largely from T-wave oversensing. The early S-ICD trials, EFFORTLESS and IDE, demonstrated device effectiveness, but inappropriate shock rates were high, with 1-year rates of 8.1% for EFFORTLESS and 13.1% for IDE [9]. Iterative discrimination and sensing algorithms addressed this [10,11], culminating in the SMART Pass high-pass filter [12]. The UNTOUCHED study tested contemporary programming in a sicker population; all 1,111 patients had an indication for primary prevention and left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less, and reported the lowest 1-year inappropriate-shock rate reported to date for a multicenter S-ICD study [13]. The Post-Approval Study confirmed real-world performance, with a 1-year IAS rate of 6.9% but only 3.1% annually over the course of the trial [14].

## Randomized Comparison With Transvenous Therapy

The pivotal PRAETORIAN trial randomized 849 patients with a class I or IIa indication for ICD therapy without the need for pacing to either S-ICD or TV-ICD therapy, followed for a median of 49.1 months [15,16]. The S-ICD met its noninferiority endpoint for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [16]. The PRAETORIAN-XL extension is now assessing whether the S-ICD is superior to the TV-ICD with respect to device-related complications at 8-year follow-up [17]. The ATLAS trial then enrolled younger and higher-risk patients; a composite of major lead-related outcomes had occurred in one S-ICD recipient and 12 TV-ICD recipients by 6 months, a 92% relative reduction with the S-ICD [18,19], though there was a numerically higher rate of inappropriate shocks with the subcutaneous device [18]. A systematic review and meta-analysis subsequently synthesized randomized and propensity-matched evidence comparing the two strategies [20].

## Patient Selection, Screening, and Defibrillation Testing

Appropriate candidate selection relies on pre-implant electrocardiographic screening and optimal device positioning. The PRAETORIAN score was developed as a tool to evaluate the implant position and predict defibrillation success of the S-ICD, based on clinical and computer-modeling knowledge of determinants affecting the defibrillation threshold: subcoil fat, subgenerator fat, and anterior positioning of the generator [21]. The PRAETORIAN-DFT trial then randomized 965 patients between defibrillation testing and PRAETORIAN score calculation after de novo S-ICD implantation to determine whether routine testing can be safely omitted [22,23]. Current ESC guidelines incorporate the S-ICD as an alternative to the TV-ICD in patients without a pacing, resynchronization, or antitachycardia-pacing indication [24], consistent with prior AHA/ACC/HRS recommendations [25].

## Limitations and Future Directions

The principal limitation of the S-ICD remains its inability to pace. Because of the lack of endocardial pacing components, patients with long-term pacing needs are ineligible for the S-ICD, and reliance on far-field sensing can hamper appropriate arrhythmia detection [26]. Two complementary technologies aim to overcome this. The extravascular ICD uses a single lead implanted substernally to enable pause-prevention pacing, antitachycardia pacing, and defibrillation energy similar to that of transvenous ICDs, and its pivotal study confirmed safe implantation and effective termination of induced arrhythmias [27]. Separately, a modular system pairs the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker [28]; in the MODULAR ATP trial, the leadless pacemaker in wireless communication with a subcutaneous ICD exceeded performance goals for freedom from major complications, for communication between devices, and for pacing threshold at 6 months [29,30].

## Conclusion

Over fifteen years, the S-ICD has evolved from a feasibility concept to a guideline-endorsed alternative to the transvenous ICD for patients without pacing indications, validated by two randomized trials. Refined sensing has minimized inappropriate shocks, and emerging extravascular and modular leadless-pacing technologies promise to extend extravascular therapy to patients who require pacing, broadening the population that can avoid endocardial leads.
